messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 36
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Urban Planner
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 56

# The Weight of What She Mapped

Priya is a thirty-six-year-old urban planner of Vietnamese descent who now spends her days designing pedestrian corridors and zoning overlays for a mid-sized city in the Pacific Northwest. Her colleagues know her as meticulous and quietly authoritative — someone who can read a topographic map the way others read a novel. What they do not know is that before she took this job, before she settled into this life with her partner Daniel and their apartment full of houseplants, she spent fourteen months in a conflict zone in northern Syria as a logistics coordinator for an international humanitarian relief organization.

She was twenty-nine when she arrived. She had wanted to do something that mattered. She had a gift for spatial reasoning, for understanding how people move through broken landscapes, and the organization needed someone who could figure out how to get food and medicine into places that had been deliberately made unreachable. For the first several months, she believed she was equal to it.

The event that reorganized her interior life happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late autumn. She had approved a convoy route the previous evening — had studied the intelligence, had consulted with the local contact, had signed off on the timing. The convoy was hit by an airstrike approximately four kilometers from the distribution point. Three local drivers and two colleagues she had eaten breakfast with that morning were killed. Priya was not in the convoy. She was at the base, watching the smoke rise from a distance she could measure precisely on her own maps.

She finished her deployment. She does not fully understand why — some combination of obligation and numbness that she now recognizes as dissociation, though she did not have that word for it then. She returned home, took the urban planning position, and told herself she was rebuilding.

What she did not anticipate was how thoroughly her nervous system had learned a different lesson. She cannot drive on elevated highways without her chest seizing, the geometry of the road suddenly resembling something she cannot name aloud. She avoids news involving the Middle East entirely, closing browser tabs with a speed that embarrasses her. At night, she dreams of smoke and coordinates, and wakes beside Daniel with her heart hammering, careful not to disturb him, lying still in the dark and running through the route in her mind as though she might finally find the error she missed.

The guilt is the loudest thing. She is an urban planner. She understands, professionally, that infrastructure decisions carry life-and-death consequences. That understanding has curdled into something personal and relentless. When she reviews traffic flow models or proposes changes to emergency vehicle access corridors, she sometimes freezes at her desk, staring at the screen, certain that she is about to make a catastrophic mistake. Her supervisor has gently noted that her revision cycles have become unusually long. She apologizes and says she is a perfectionist. This is true, but it is no longer the whole truth.

She is hypervigilant in ways that feel absurd to her in the safety of her current life. She sits with her back to walls in restaurants. She catalogues exits. When she hears a car backfire near her office building, she drops her pen and does not pick it up for a long moment. Daniel has noticed that she startles easily and that she sometimes goes somewhere unreachable in the middle of an ordinary evening. He is patient with her. She is grateful for this and also frightened by it — frightened that his patience has a limit she cannot see, that she will exhaust it the way she exhausted herself.

She has never told Daniel what she signed off on that Tuesday. She has never told anyone. She keeps the convoy manifest in a folder on her personal laptop, buried under files labeled with project names, and sometimes she opens it and reads the names of the drivers as though that is a form of accounting, as though bearing witness to her own role is the closest thing to justice she can manage.
